lesson.title: Ethernet: From Shared Coaxial Cable to the De Facto Wired Standard
lesson.summary: Ethernet is the IEEE 802.3 family of standards that defined both the CSMA/CD access method for early shared media and the frame format still used today, and its evolution from a single shared cable to switched, full duplex links explains why collision handling matters far less on a modern wired LAN than it once did.
lesson.body:
Ethernet began at Xerox PARC in the 1970s as a way to let many workstations share a single coaxial cable, and it was standardized by the IEEE as the 802.3 family, one member of the broader IEEE 802 set of LAN standards that also produced 802.11 for Wi-Fi. In its original form, Ethernet's defining feature at the MAC layer was exactly the CSMA/CD access method: any station could sense the shared cable, transmit when it appeared idle, and detect and abort a collision if one occurred, backing off and retrying with the binary exponential backoff scheme. That combination, a common bus topology plus CSMA/CD arbitration, is what the name Ethernet originally meant in practice.

The Ethernet frame format, defined by the 802.3 standard, is the other half of what makes Ethernet Ethernet, and it has stayed relatively stable even as the underlying medium changed completely. A frame carries a preamble for receiver synchronization, destination and source MAC addresses so stations can filter frames meant for them, exactly the MAC address use case that motivated media access control in the first place, a field identifying the upper layer protocol or the frame's length, the payload itself, and a trailing frame check sequence, a CRC, that lets the receiver detect corruption, the same error detection role that underlies every ARQ scheme discussed earlier in this unit. The minimum frame size constraint from CSMA/CD, 64 bytes, is enforced at exactly this framing layer, with padding added if the actual payload is too short.

The physical topology of Ethernet changed dramatically even while the frame format held steady. Shared coaxial cable gave way to hubs wired in a star topology but still electrically equivalent to a shared bus, meaning every station still contended for the same collision domain and CSMA/CD still mattered. The real break came with switches: an Ethernet switch gives each connected device its own dedicated point to point link and forwards frames only to the port where the destination MAC address actually lives, rather than broadcasting every frame to everyone the way a hub did. Once every link is a private connection between exactly two devices, there is no shared medium left for multiple stations to contend over on that link at all.

Switching also enabled full duplex operation, sending and receiving simultaneously on separate wire pairs, which is physically incompatible with CSMA/CD's core assumption that a station can only be doing one of the two at a time and must monitor the medium for a collision while sending. On a full duplex switched link between exactly two devices, in fact, collisions are structurally impossible: there is no other station to collide with, and CSMA/CD is simply disabled. Nearly all modern wired Ethernet installations, in offices, homes, and data centers, run this way, which is why the elaborate exponential backoff and jam signal machinery of CSMA/CD, still formally part of the 802.3 standard, sits largely dormant in practice today.

Ethernet's staying power over four decades of speed increases, from the original 10 megabits per second to modern multi gigabit links, owes less to CSMA/CD, which effectively retired itself once switching took over, and more to the stability of its addressing and framing model built on MAC addresses and a well defined frame check sequence. It stands as a useful closing example for this unit: a named standard can outlive the specific media access discipline it was originally built around, once the assumption that access needs to be shared and arbitrated at all quietly stops being true.
